newsitem.title: CANADA: Bre-X whodunit revives Klondike gold rush memories.
newsitem.headline: Bre-X whodunit revives Klondike gold rush memories.

text.p: The saga of Canada's Bre-X Minerals Ltd. and its worthless Indonesian gold field has become a national whodunit and revived memories of the great Klondike gold rush over a century ago.
As Canadian Mounties probe the biggest swindle in mining history, the Busang fiasco is dominating conversations in pubs and offices and on streetcorners across the country.
The rags-to-riches-to-rags story has all the elements of a Hitchcock thriller -- a mysterious death, international intrigue, a jungle setting, greed and gold.

Several books are planned on the suspenseful yarn of the former stock market darling that sank into oblivion after a damning report concluded that Busang -- once touted as the world's richest gold find -- was a massive fraud.
"It's a real man-on-the-street story. It has touched everybody," said Brad Martin, president of Penguin Books Canada Ltd., which will publish a Bre-X book in 1998.

"You could be standing in an elevator or a bar and hear about somebody related to someone who bought Bre-X and made huge amounts of money. Now the story is 'I know someone who lost a tremendous amount of money,'" Martin said.
The Bre-X caper is a classic example of truth being stranger than fiction.

The cast of characters includes Bre-X's once-bankrupt chairman, David Walsh, who gambled his last C$10,000 ($7,200) on Busang, earned millions of dollars from stock options as the shares soared from pennies to over C$28 ($21) and now claims his company was defrauded by unnamed parties.
Thousands of miles away in the Cayman Islands, Bre-X's chain-smoking former exploration chief, John Felderhof, is in virtual seclusion on his $2.9 million estate.
Felderhof, who was fired by Bre-X last week, has denied any wrongdoing in the Busang affair.

Rumors continue to swirl around Bre-X's No. 2 geologist, Michael de Guzman, who apparently committed suicide by jumping from a helicopter over the Borneo jungle and left a suicide note to one of his four wives. De Guzman, who some believe is still alive, disappeared just a few days before negative assays on Busang from partner Freeport-McMoRan Copper & Gold Inc. sparked a selloff of Bre-X stock in March.

Rounding out the cast are Freeport's flamboyant Texas-born Chief Executive Jim Bob Moffett, Indonesian President Suharto, former President George Bush and retired Canadian Prime Minister Brian Mulroney.
Bush and Mulroney were advisers to Barrick Gold Corp. Chairman Peter Munk in his unsuccessful bid to wrest control of Busang from tiny Bre-X last year.
Historians see parallels between gold fever in Canada's Yukon over 100 years ago and the frenzy over Busang.

"Indonesia. The Klondike. It's somewhere foreign and totally strange, and that adds to the mystery and the allure of the story," Mac Swackhammer, museum curator in Dawson City, Yukon, said in a telephone interview.
George Carmack and his Indian brothers-in-law Skookum Jim and Tagish Charley made the 19th century's last big gold strike near the Klondike River in the summer of 1896.
News of the discovery spread by steamship to the American West Coast, touching off a stampede of prospectors, miners, merchants and adventurers in search of the mother lode.
"Klondic-itis" jolted the economy out of depression as people used hoarded funds to finance expeditions. By winter, 100,000 gold seekers were off for Northern Canada and Alaska.

"Other stampedes involved more gold and more men, but there had been nothing like the Klondike before, there has been nothing like it since, and there can never be anything like it again," Canadian author Pierre Berton wrote in his book on the era, "Klondike."
Dawson City grew overnight into the biggest town north of Seattle and west of Winnipeg, with electricity, telephones, two banks, movie theaters, saloons and dance halls.
Prostitution was tolerated, but gambling was outlawed on Sundays. Law and order was enforced by Sam Steele, a tough, barrel-chested Mountie known as the "Lion of the Yukon."
Of the 40,000 gold seekers who made it to the Klondike, only 4,000 miners found any gold, while maybe 100 got rich. Only a few held on to their wealth.
In between, there were many scams and false claims.

One fools' rush was sparked by an old sea dog who claimed to have found "nuggets as big as hickory nuts" at Kotzebue Sound, about 500 miles (800 km) north of the Klondike. Over 1,000 miners flocked to the sound and left empty-handed.
Bre-X gold fever was equally infectious, luring stock market amateurs to bet their life savings on the promise of fabulous wealth in Indonesia.

An estimated C$500 million ($365 million) was lent to people to buy Bre-X shares. Investors were forced to pay it back when the stock -- once worth C$6 billion ($4.4 billion) -- sank to pennies a share last week.
